name: Daria Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, governments or political parties. We don’t sell anything or campaign, and your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead three administrators who check maintenance invoices inside a large property company, but I'm only five months into the junior manager job after years away caring for my father. I'm 58, I've got a bachelor's degree, and I use the approved AI assistant daily; unfortunately being quick with the tool hasn't made me good at giving instructions, so my boss still corrects my allocations. My partner cleans offices part-time, our daughter and son are grown, and we rent a flat with a balcony full of the plants I keep propagating. My 2,700 take-home and his 900 cover about 3,500 a month, with 2,200 saved after recent dental bills; I'd like to finish at 67, but I haven't established what income we'd have then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues the assistant can still be useful without running the company. If it sorts the invoice descriptions and leaves us time to notice a double charge, I'll take the small saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still worry about proving I can manage, because I'm not yet getting the priorities right. There's only 100 left after a normal month, and our 2,200 reserve is less than one month of total expenses. A new tooth problem or a lost wage would upset us quickly, even if AI never did more than this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the approved invoice-description helper running during my normal paid work and keep my boss's existing sign-off for allocations. I'd ask each administrator to repeat the day's first priority at the usual morning check, so I could catch my own muddled instructions. At home I'd continue the current 100 monthly savings transfer while both wages lasted and leave the dental reserve alone, rather than pay for a premium AI account. Through the first year I'd keep the job if the company kept me, without assuming my enthusiasm earned a promotion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about making the role stick, with some enjoyment in the tools. I'm quicker at finding a new button than at knowing which request should wait until tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when the assistant labels an invoice wrongly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I correct the label against the actual invoice and don't let it approve a payment. That permission belongs to the existing approver, not to me because I can make a neat summary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children know the savings were thin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them if there was a bill we couldn't manage, rather than hint we could fund everyone's next expense. They're grown, with their own rent and plans; I don't want either side inventing money the other side hasn't got.

say: I'd value **small savings** in invoice descriptions without expecting the assistant to run the company.
I'd judge the result by catching **double charges**, not by how impressive a summary looks.
think: I worry about **proving myself** because my priorities still aren't consistently right.
Our **100 monthly surplus** and reserve below one month's total expenses leave us exposed to another bill or wage loss.
do: Keep the approved **description helper** during normal paid work, retaining existing allocation sign-off and payment authority.
Check each administrator's **first priority** at the existing morning meeting to catch muddled instructions.
Continue the current **100 monthly** savings transfer while both wages last, without buying a premium AI account.
feel: **Anxious but interested**, enjoying tools while struggling with management judgement.
S0.quote: I'm quicker at finding a new button than at knowing which request should wait until tomorrow.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** does not imply strong management skill; she explicitly relies on existing allocation and payment checks.
Her **baseline anxiety** reflects a thin reserve and performance risk, despite enjoying small practical improvements.

steps.text: Continue the approved invoice helper with existing allocation sign-off and payment checks
Clarify first priorities in the usual morning check and continue existing savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be honest that writing, checking and allocating invoices are exactly the things being automated. I'd show colleagues what I've learned, but I wouldn't tell them liking AI makes their jobs safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own junior management job is at risk because the company can automate both the checking and the allocation I still need help with. Being fast with the assistant might help me get an interview, but it's not a claim to a salary. With few similar employers nearby, a pay cut could be the price of staying employed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply this month for advertised administration and invoice roles as well as junior management, using my own time and public job information. I'd consider a longer bus journey, but accept only a signed offer leaving at least 2,700 take-home after extra travel costs, with actual shift times covered by the bus timetable; otherwise we'd need a separately agreed and funded household plan before resignation. In the first year I'd keep using our approved assistant with current checks while employed and practise explaining my work using invented examples on my own device, with no company records or paid software. I'd ask for interview leave but assume no paid interview hours unless the employer agreed them in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and restless, because sending an application is at least something I can finish. I'd have to stop myself refreshing the inbox while my own team waited for an answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you apply if the wage wasn't advertised?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but I'd ask about the actual pay and hours before accepting anything. Sending a form isn't agreeing to a wage I haven't seen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the bus condition?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner walks to the offices he cleans and we don't own a car. A better job that finishes after the last bus isn't a better household plan unless we've funded another way home.

say: I'd say **invoice tasks** are directly exposed to automation, including allocation and checking.
I'd share what I know without calling **AI enthusiasm** protection from job loss.
think: My **junior management job** is at risk because software can allocate and check work I still need help managing.
Tool speed might win an interview, but **few local employers** could make a pay cut necessary.
do: Apply for **advertised roles** now in personal time, including administration rather than only management.
Accept only **signed terms** leaving 2,700 take-home after extra travel and bus-covered shifts, unless we separately agree and fund another plan.
Practise with **invented examples** on my own device without company records or fees; count paid interview leave only after written approval.
feel: **Anxious and restless**, using applications to make progress without waiting constantly for replies.
S1.quote: Being fast with the assistant might help me get an interview, but it's not a claim to a salary.
fieldNote: Her **applications** are broader than management, but acceptance requires actual pay, workable transport and signed terms before resignation.
Her **practice** uses personal time, invented information and no paid software; interview leave is requested rather than presumed paid.

steps.text: Apply to advertised administration, invoice and junior management roles in personal time
Practise describing AI-assisted work with invented examples on her own device without fees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the family that being the person who enjoys AI doesn't mean the company needs me when it can do the thinking itself. I'd ask my partner to plan with me before we start telling each other not to worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect my wage to go around 2028 when I'd be sixty, not in 2031 when robots arrive. My partner's 900 from cleaning might last longer, but it leaves a 2,600 monthly gap at today's costs and could also be threatened by robots later. Our 2,200 isn't enough for a month of that gap, and no pension entitlement at sixty is confirmed. I'd be frightened even while I kept moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my sister now whether she'd consider us sharing her home temporarily if my job ended, without assuming she'd agree or moving on a verbal suggestion. We'd move only after a written household agreement, any required landlord permission and a costed plan for deposits, transport and monthly contributions that used confirmed money rather than a new wage we hoped for. In the first year after AGI, if my pay stopped, I'd seek eligible income support and ask our landlord about temporary rent relief while checking actual pension and leaving entitlements. If my sister couldn't help, we'd stay put while seeking those answers; no rent saving or support payment belongs in our budget before approval and actual dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and likely to be awake composing a message to my sister instead of sending it. I'm quick with an application screen and slow about asking my own family for a room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually write to your sister?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask if she had time for a conversation about temporary sharing and say she could decline. I wouldn't write that we'd already decided to come or that she could cover costs she hadn't seen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could another office job solve the gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, but I wouldn't call the same thinking tasks under another company name safe from AGI. Any offered wage would need signed terms and a workable travel budget before I counted it.

say: I'd explain that **enjoying AI** doesn't make me necessary when the company can buy the thinking cheaply.
I'd ask my **partner** to plan with me rather than exchange empty reassurance.
think: At **sixty**, I expect my wage to go before robots, with no confirmed pension available.
My partner's **900** leaves a 2,600 monthly gap our 2,200 can't cover for a month; later robots could threaten his income.
do: Ask my **sister** about temporary sharing without assuming agreement, space or money.
Move only with **written household terms**, required landlord permission and funded deposits, transport and monthly contributions using confirmed money.
Request **eligible support**, rent relief and pension/leaving terms after wage loss; count no payments or rent savings before approval and dates.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, finding it harder to request a family room than complete an application screen.
S2.quote: I'm quick with an application screen and slow about asking my own family for a room.
fieldNote: Her **family move** requires agreement, permission and a funded plan rather than assuming her sister has free accommodation available.
The **2,600 shortfall** compares household costs with the current cleaning wage; neither support, pension nor a replacement office job is presumed.

steps.text: Ask her sister about temporary sharing without assuming agreement or financial help
Move only after written household terms, permission and a funded cost-and-transport plan
Request eligible support and temporary rent relief after wage loss

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us test a small source of earnings without pretending the first sale replaces a job. I'd ask people at church what they'd actually buy, rather than announce I was starting a nursery because I own some plant pots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 63 and expect my invoice role to go in 2031, even if I'd learned every feature of the assistant. Selling a few plants might give me a little income and something I enjoy, but buyers without wages might stop buying. Robots around 2034 could change the growing and selling too, so this isn't a protected trade I've discovered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the church market organiser about stall permission and fees now, then offer one small batch of propagated plants in my own weekend time only if permission and any local selling rules were confirmed. I'd spend at most 60 from one month's 100 surplus, including a stall fee capped at 10, leaving our 2,200 savings untouched; I'd only prepare stock after paid orders covered those direct costs, with clear refund terms if I couldn't supply. In the first year after AGI I'd repeat a batch only after recording all costs and actual receipts from the first, count only realised profit as income, and keep applying for paid work after any salary loss. I'd request pension figures during the preparation years too, without assuming age 63 gave access or plant sales could cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about the main wage, and interested in the little experiment without confusing the two. A tray of seedlings can be a sale; it isn't a retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the stall costs 25 rather than 10?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd decline that market under this plan, rather than quietly take the difference from savings. I could ask about another permitted stall, but I'd need to redo the costed order offer before taking anybody's money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy more growing equipment after a good first day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after checking the profit after every cost and agreeing another capped batch from money we actually had. I wouldn't borrow or spend the household reserve because somebody said my plants looked lovely.

say: I'd test **small earnings** without claiming a first sale replaces a job.
I'd ask people what they'd buy rather than call a few **plant pots** a nursery business.
think: At **63**, I expect my invoice job to go regardless of assistant fluency.
Possible **plant income** faces weak demand and later robots, so it isn't a protected trade or certain household wage.
do: Confirm **stall permission** and selling rules before offering plants; prepare stock only after paid orders cover direct costs under clear refund terms.
Cap total **batch costs at 60**, including a stall fee up to 10, using one month's surplus while leaving 2,200 untouched.
Repeat only after checking **profit after every cost** and agreeing another capped batch from actual money, without borrowing or household reserves.
feel: **Alarmed but interested**, separating a small experiment from the endangered main wage.
S3.quote: A tray of seedlings can be a sale; it isn't a retirement plan.
fieldNote: Her **plant experiment** has permission, prepaid cost coverage, a total loss cap and a separate repeat decision rather than assumed ongoing sales.
She protects the **2,200 reserve**, counts only realised profit and recognises both demand risk and the later robot timetable.

steps.text: Offer one plant batch only under permission, prepaid-cost, refund and 60 total-cost gates
Apply for paid work after salary loss without assuming pension access or sufficient plant profits
Repeat only after checking net profit and agreeing another capped batch without borrowing or household reserves

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives me a chance to finish working on my own terms, but only if I check what finishing would pay. I'd encourage the children to learn how to read pension statements now, rather than wait until a birthday makes the question urgent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 68 in 2036, a year after the 67 I'd hoped to stop at, so the dates could line up better for us. I don't know whether the income would cover our rent, and my partner's cleaner wage wouldn't be guaranteed beyond the robots around 2039. I'm less frightened by this picture, but I can't call an age a bank transfer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the pension schemes for written payable dates and amounts after deductions now, and take them to a no-fee community appointment only after the service confirmed it was free. I'd keep working and saving the existing 100 monthly while both wages and our health lasted, then review the budget with my partner each year. We'd stop relying on my wage at 67 only after confirmed retirement income covered actual costs and a separately identified allowance for unexpected bills; otherwise I'd delay stopping and seek actual paid vacancies or eligible support. In the first year after AGI I'd recheck income, rent and support eligibility rather than assume a retirement decision could never need revisiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with some room to look forward rather than race ahead of a deadline. I'd like to retire because the sums work, not because I've run out of job titles to apply for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you bring retirement earlier than 67 if AGI looked certain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not just because of the forecast; 67 is already the age I'd been hoping for. Any earlier date would need its own funded plan, and I don't have one to announce.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep the plant sales going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a real test had shown a profit and we still wanted to do it; I wouldn't put hypothetical sales in the pension column. I'd rather treat a good batch as extra money than use it to justify an unaffordable leaving date.

say: I'd say **finishing work** needs a check of the income afterward, even with a decade to prepare.
I'd encourage my **grown children** to learn to read pension statements before birthdays make the question urgent.
think: At **68**, AGI could arrive after my hoped-for stopping age of 67, but the rent still needs confirmed income.
My partner's **cleaner wage** also faces later robot exposure, so an age isn't a payment guarantee.
do: Request written **pension dates** and net amounts and use community advice only after confirming no fee.
Continue the existing **100 monthly** saving while wages and health last, reviewing the household budget annually.
Stop at **67 only** when confirmed retirement income covers costs and unexpected bills; otherwise delay, seek vacancies or eligible support, and reassess.
feel: **Anxious but less frightened**, able to look forward without declaring the retirement funded.
S4.quote: I'd like to retire because the sums work, not because I've run out of job titles to apply for.
fieldNote: Her **age arithmetic** is explicit: 58 now, 68 at AGI, with an existing hoped-for date of 67 rather than newly early retirement.
Her **retirement gate** excludes hypothetical plant profit and requires actual income, costs and unexpected-bill provision, with later reassessment.

steps.text: Request no-fee community help interpreting written pension dates and net payments
Continue the existing 100 monthly saving while wages and health last
Seek real vacancies if confirmed retirement income cannot cover costs and unexpected bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be sixty and our main wage could be gone before a pension was available. I'd want clear notice, access to paid job interviews before departure, and a pension statement with actual payable dates and amounts; none of those wages or payments is agreed now. I can learn another tool overnight; I can't grow a spare salary overnight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether somebody's good with AI or good at being a manager, because those aren't the same. I like trying the tools and I still sometimes give three people the same priority without saying what can wait. I want to earn my place, not be congratulated for clicking faster.

headlineQuote: I can learn another tool overnight; I can't grow a spare salary overnight.
portrait: Daria is **58**, a junior manager with a bachelor's degree returning after caring for her father, still learning to direct three administrators.
She uses **AI daily**, but her boss still corrects work allocations; tool fluency hasn't made her an expert manager.
She and her **cleaner partner** rent, have grown children and 2,200 saved against 3,500 monthly costs after dental bills.
Her **experiments** are quick and bounded, while job acceptance, a possible seedling business and hoped-for retirement at 67 remain conditional.
biggestWorry: I fear **AGI by 2028** most because I'd be sixty and the main wage might go before pension access.
whatWouldHelp: I need **clear notice**, paid interview access before departure and confirmed pension ages and amounts.
